You are able to perfectly restore any continuous signal from discrete samples as long as the sampling rate/frequency is at least twice the highest frequency in your signal. The human ear frequency range is usually up to 20kHz - that is the reason most audio formats sampling rates are ~40kHz. The frequency of human speech is much lower than 20kHz so if you care only about speech you can sample it slower (equal to speeding it up) | Why not run a local instance of whisper small or medium ? | Is this just a screenshot or is there a link? Quick Hack: Save up to 99% tokens in Codex fire One of the biggest hidden sources of token usage in agent workflows is command output. Things like: test results logs stack traces CLI tools Can easily generate thousands of tokens, even when the LLM only needs to answer something simple like: >“Did the tests pass?” To experiment with this, I built a small tool with Claude called distill. The idea is simple: Instead of sending the entire command output to the LLM, a small local model summarizes the result into only the information the LLM actually needs. Example: > > Instead of sending thousands of tokens of test logs, the LLM receives something like: >All tests passed In some cases this reduces the payload by \~99% tokens while preserving the signal needed for reasoning. Codex helped me design the architecture and iterate on the CLI behavior. The project is open source and free to try if anyone wants to experiment with token reduction strategies in agent workflows. | This is clever. How to get Codex to create proper UIs out of gpt-image-2 mock ups I often read here how people think gpt-image-2 is amazing for creating mockups, but then struggle to recreate them with Codex. This is because people do this: "Create a UI mockup for 'Teams but good'" -> Bot generates image -> "And now create a web app with this design" And then you probably get something non-responsive, maybe even borderline broken. No human frontend guy would work this way, so the bot will not produce good results this way either. A human frontend guy would take the mockup and first build a design system out of it, specifying every control, every layout choice, every color, and whatnot. Then he implements the design system, and the mockup is basically just a single realization of that design system. So, easy solution: Do the same with Codex. Ask gpt-image-2 to create a design system out of the mockup, then tell Codex to implement the design system. Or even better: tell it to research a UI framework that is already pretty close to what you want. That saves plenty of time and is generally better for the final result than having the bot implement every control or whatnot on its own. Then, after the design system is implemented, it should build the UI. Another big advantage of this approach: fine-grained control over editing the design. "Please change the colors in the system to xxxxx" will result in much more coherent theming than taking the mockup as the base and asking, "Make it more pink." Sa
